title: Register shifts in speech and writing
objectives: Contrast formal and conversational grammatical choices.
Rewrite requests and relative clauses for a specified context.
Recognise when a register shift changes the intended meaning.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Register is the choice of language suited to a situation, audience and purpose. A message to a friend, a customer-service reply and a research report can all use standard English while favouring different grammatical choices. Formality is not a scale of grammatical correctness: “Who did you speak to?” is standard and natural in conversation, while “To whom did you speak?” is more formal.

A successful register shift preserves the relevant message while changing its presentation. It may replace a contraction with a full form, make a request less direct, or choose a more explicit connection. The writer must also consider the relationship with the audience; an overly elaborate email can sound distant.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Contractions are common in speech and informal writing: “We can’t attend.” A formal report may prefer “We cannot attend.” Both express the same negative modal meaning here. In formal relative clauses, a preposition can precede whom or which: “the colleague to whom I spoke”. In everyday speech, a final preposition is natural: “the colleague I spoke to”.

Requests can use different levels of directness. “Send the file” is a direct imperative; “Could you send the file?” is an indirect question used as a request. Tone, relationship and context all affect politeness, so no single structure guarantees a polite effect in every situation.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare an informal update, “The tests didn’t work, so we’ll try again”, with “The tests were unsuccessful; consequently, we will repeat them.” The second uses full forms and a formal linking adverb. It preserves the intended sequence and outcome, although it may be unnecessarily formal for a quick message to a close colleague.

A speaker may use ellipsis where a formal document needs fuller reference: “Finished?” “Almost.” In a report, “The review is almost complete” identifies the subject and state. Passive voice and nominalisation can also be useful, but they should not obscure the actor when identifying that actor matters.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not “correct” a stranded preposition solely because a formal alternative exists. Both “the person I spoke to” and “the person to whom I spoke” are grammatical. The second may be inappropriate for a very casual exchange because of its register, not because it violates grammar.

A change in wording must preserve the intended force. “You must send the file” expresses obligation; “You could send the file” may express a suggestion. Replacing one with the other merely to sound polite can change the instruction. Choose a form that fits both the relationship and the actual requirement.

examples.note: A final preposition is standard and natural in conversation.
The fronted preposition sounds more formal.
The contraction is common in informal communication.
The full form can suit formal writing.
A question form can make a request less direct.
An imperative makes a direct request or instruction.

examples.sentence: The tests failed; consequently, we will repeat them.
examples.note: Consequently presents the second action as a result in formal prose.

common_errors.incorrect: The colleague to who I spoke replied.
common_errors.correct: The colleague to whom I spoke replied.
common_errors.reason: Whom follows the fronted preposition in this formal pattern.
Could takes the base verb send.

common_errors.incorrect: The tests failed; consequently, we will repeats them.
common_errors.correct: The tests failed; consequently, we will repeat them.
common_errors.reason: Will takes the base form repeat.

summary: Register choices depend on audience, purpose and relationship.
Conversational and formal structures can both be standard.
Preserve meaning and force when changing register.
